title: The Garage Fire That Sent Chung Ju-yung Back to His Moneylender
dek: In 1940, weeks after taking over a Seoul repair shop on borrowed money, the future Hyundai founder lost it to fire and went back to borrow again.

story.event: Rebuilding his first car-repair garage on fresh borrowing after it burned down weeks after opening
story.summary: In 1940, after colonial rice controls closed his Seoul rice shop, Chung Ju-yung took over a small repair garage, A-do (Art) Service, with borrowed money. Within weeks a fire destroyed the building and customers' vehicles; he borrowed again, paid the owners for their cars and restarted in a makeshift shed in the Dongdaemun area. The garage grew until the colonial government forced it into a merger in 1943, and in 1946 he opened Hyundai Motor Service Center.
paragraphs: In December 1939 a new rice distribution policy of the Japanese colonial government closed every Korean-run rice shop, Chung Ju-yung's Kyungil Rice Store in Seoul among them. In the spring of 1940, looking for a trade the controls did not reach, he took the advice of Lee Eul-hak, a mechanic he knew, and took over a small repair works called A-do Service, from the English "Art Service". He paid with money borrowed from friends and a moneylender. The historian Andrei Lankov notes that he had no experience of cars at all.

Work arrived from the first day. Jeon Young-sun, a historian of Korean motoring, writes that within twenty days Chung had repaid half of what he had borrowed and the rest of the purchase price. A few days later, at dawn, the garage caught fire; by Jeon's account a worker who had worked through the night lit thinner to heat water for washing his greasy hands. The building burned, and with it several trucks under repair and an Oldsmobile belonging to Yun Deok-yeong, an uncle of Korea's last empress.

Chung now owed his lenders and the owners of the burned vehicles, and he had no workshop. According to Jeon, he went back to the moneylender who had lent to him before and pleaded for more. The lender, who trusted his record, lent him another 1,000 won. Chung spent it paying the owners for their vehicles, which left nothing for a new garage. So he rented a small empty plot in a back street of Sinseol-dong, in the Dongdaemun area, put up a wooden shed barely big enough to take the front of a car, and began repairing engines there without a licence.

The business recovered. Within three years its staff grew from about twenty to about seventy, and its name rested on speed; Chung later said, "we repaired in only five days what took other companies twenty". In 1943 the colonial government forced the garage into a merger to serve the war effort, and he lost it. In April 1946, after liberation, he opened a new repair shop in central Seoul under the sign Hyundai Motor Service Center, the first business to carry the name.

quote.text: It would be some consolation for the feebleness of our selves and our works, if all things should perish as slowly as they come into being; but as it is, increases are of sluggish growth, but the way to ruin is rapid.
quote.work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium)
quote.locator: Letter XCI, "On the Lesson to be Drawn from the Burning of Lyons", section 6
quote.translator: Richard M. Gummere (Loeb Classical Library, volume 2, 1920)
quote.source_title: Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 91, tr. Richard M. Gummere (Wikisource)
quote.connection: Seneca wrote this after fire destroyed the city of Lyons in a single night. Chung's garage took twenty days to start paying its way and one early morning to burn. What Seneca leaves unsaid, and the story supplies, is that the slow part can be started again when someone still trusts you.

reflection: Nearly everything Chung owned burned in one morning. What survived was harder to see: a moneylender's sense, built over years of repaid debts and delivered rice, that this young man would pay. That was the slow kind of growth Seneca had in mind, and the fire did not touch it. Notice, too, whom Chung paid first: the people whose cars he had lost.

You are building some of that slow thing now, mostly in moments that feel too small to count: a reply sent when you said it would be, a mistake owned before anyone found it. On a tired day it is easy to think only the visible work matters. The less visible kind is what people lend against when something goes wrong.
invitation: Think of one small promise you made this week, to a colleague, a client or someone at home, that is still open. Keep it today, or tell that person plainly when you will.

sources.title: Biography: Chung Ju-yung (Repairing cars: the root of Hyundai)
sources.supports: Kyungil Rice Store opened January 1938 and closed in December 1939 under the Government-General's rice distribution policy; return to Seoul the following spring and takeover of the Art Service Garage at the invitation of Lee Ul Hak; business flourished from opening day; fire within twenty days destroying the building, five trucks under repair and an Oldsmobile; the debt that followed; borrowing more on the strength of his trustworthiness and starting a repair works in Dongdaemun; forced merger with a Japanese company in 1943; Hyundai Motor Service Center opened in April 1946 in Seoul and gave the group its name.

sources.title: [Jeon Young-sun's Auto Museum] The root of Hyundai Motor: the A-do Service works (1) (in Korean)
sources.publisher: Segye Ilbo (syndicated from Top Rider; Jeon Young-sun, 14 September 2010)
sources.supports: Rice shop forced to close in 1939 when free rice sales were banned; Chung looking for a business beyond Japanese controls; the mechanic Lee Eul-hak's advice; takeover in 1940 of the small A-do Service (Art Service) works in Bukahyeon-dong, with money borrowed from a friend and a moneylender; repaying half the borrowed money and the balance of the price within twenty days of opening; the dawn fire five days later, started by a worker heating water with thinner; three trucks and Yun Deok-yeong's Oldsmobile destroyed and two trucks outside half-burned; not enough money to compensate the owners; the moneylender's further loan of 1,000 won, used to compensate them; restarting in a tiny wooden shed on rented land in a back street of Sinseol-dong, without a licence.

sources.title: (5) Chung Ju-yung: embodiment of Korea's economic miracle
sources.supports: Loss of the rice business in 1939; in 1940 Chung borrowed money from affluent friends and opened a small repair shop in Seoul with no experience of cars; the garage closed by the authorities in 1943 without compensation; reopening after liberation in 1946 under the name Hyundai.

cross_checks.claim: Chung's rice shop was closed in late 1939 under colonial rice controls, before he moved into car repair.
In 1940 he took over a small Seoul repair garage with borrowed money.
Within weeks of opening, fire destroyed the garage building, trucks under repair and an Oldsmobile.
He borrowed more money and restarted the business in the Dongdaemun area (Sinseol-dong).
The garage was taken from him in 1943 by the colonial authorities, through a forced merger.
In 1946, after liberation, he opened a repair shop under the Hyundai name.

research_notes: The slate called this a car-repair shop that burned in 1940; that holds, but the detail comes mainly from two sources: the official biography at the Asan Chung Ju-yung Museum and a 2010 Segye Ilbo column (in Korean) by the motoring historian Jeon Young-sun. Chung's own autobiography (English edition, Born of This Land) has a chapter titled 'An auto-repair shop, a fire, and Ado Service again', but only its contents page could be read, so no words of his about the fire are quoted. Differences: (1) Year: the museum, Jeon and Lankov (Korea Times) put the takeover in 1940; Hyundai Motor Europe's heritage page says 1941. The story uses 1940. (2) Money: Jeon says the garage cost 3,500 won, borrowed partly from a friend and a moneylender; Lankov says money borrowed from affluent friends; Wikipedia (not cited) says a 3,000 won loan. The story gives no purchase figure and says friends and a moneylender. (3) Timing of the fire: the museum says it came 'just in twenty days'; Jeon says twenty days after opening Chung repaid half his loans and the fire came five days after that. The story says 'within twenty days' for the repayment and 'a few days later' for the fire. (4) Vehicles: the museum says five trucks under repair and an Oldsmobile; Jeon says three trucks and Yun Deok-yeong's Oldsmobile burned and two trucks outside were half burned. The story says 'several trucks'. (5) The cause of the fire, the 1,000 won second loan, paying the owners first and the Sinseol-dong shed rest on Jeon alone and are attributed to him; the museum independently confirms the further borrowing and the restart in Dongdaemun (Sinseol-dong lies in Dongdaemun district). (6) Names: the museum romanises the mechanic as Lee Ul Hak; the story uses Lee Eul-hak from Jeon's Korean. The garage appears as A-do or Ado Service (Wikipedia, the autobiography) and Art Service (the museum, and Jeon's gloss). (7) 1943: Lankov says the authorities closed the garage without compensation; the museum says it was forced to merge with a Japanese company; Hyundai Motor Europe says it was merged with a steel mill for the war effort. The story says a forced merger to serve the war effort, after which he lost it. (8) Rice shop: the museum says Korean rice shops were closed under the December 1939 distribution policy; Lankov says the business was confiscated in 1939; Jeon says free sale of rice was banned. The story follows the museum. The Segye page is in Korean and does not name Chung in Latin script, so the source checker marks it as loading but not naming him. Seneca's letter consoles his friend Liberalis after the fire at Lyons (Lugdunum); it is applied here by analogy.
